scenes.sub: Because std::remove doesn't actually remove anything.
scenes.say: The erase remove idiom. It exists because of one surprising fact: the remove algorithm doesn't actually remove anything.

scenes.head: Watch remove, then erase
scenes.say: Remove two from one, two, three, two, five. Here's the surprise: remove doesn't erase anything. It can't. It only sees iterators, not the vector. Instead it shifts the keepers forward. Three moves into slot one, five moves into slot two. It returns an iterator to the new logical end. Past it are leftovers, with unspecified values, and the size is still five. Then erase, from it to the end, actually destroys them and shrinks the vector to three.

scenes.head: The idiom, and the modern shortcut
scenes.say: Put together, that's the erase remove idiom, in one line. Remove if does the same with a condition. It's one pass, O of n, with each kept element moved at most once. Erasing matches one at a time instead would be O of n squared, since every erase shifts the tail. In C plus plus twenty you can simply call erase or erase if on the container, and they do the idiom for you.

scenes.head: The classic trap

panels.code:
v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2));            // BUG
v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2), v.end());   // OK

std::list<int> l = {1, 2, 3, 2};
l.remove(2);   // list member: unlinks nodes directly

scenes.say: The classic trap: forgetting the second argument. Then erase removes just one element, the first leftover. And if nothing matched, remove returns end, and erasing end is undefined behavior. Always pass v dot end as the second argument. And for a list, use its member function remove instead. It unlinks the nodes directly, without moving any values around.

lines: std::remove only shifts keepers forward and returns the new logical end.
v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()) then actually shrinks the container.
C++20: std::erase / std::erase_if. Don't forget the second argument to erase.
scenes.say: Remove only shifts the keepers forward and returns the new logical end. Erase then cuts off the leftovers. In C plus plus twenty, just call erase or erase if. And never forget the second argument to erase.
